questions.stem: What happens to the cervix during labour?

options.text: It closes completely to keep the baby inside
It dilates (widens) to allow the baby to pass through
It becomes thicker to protect the baby
It detaches from the uterus

questions.explanation: During labour, the cervix gradually dilates (opens) from about 0 cm to approximately 10 cm. This dilation is necessary to allow the baby to pass from the uterus through the birth canal (vagina).

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates contractions of the uterus during labour?

options.text: Oxytocin
Insulin
Oestrogen
Progesterone

questions.explanation: Oxytocin is released from the pituitary gland and causes the muscular walls of the uterus to contract during labour. As contractions become stronger and more frequent, they push the baby towards and through the cervix.

questions.stem: The control of labour by oxytocin is an example of which type of feedback?

options.text: Positive feedback
Negative feedback
No feedback mechanism is involved
Hormonal feedback

questions.explanation: Labour is controlled by positive feedback. Contractions push the baby against the cervix, which stimulates more oxytocin release, causing stronger contractions. This cycle continues until the baby is born, ending the stimulus.

options.text: The placenta and membranes, expelled after the baby is born
The amniotic fluid released before birth
The umbilical cord that is cut at birth
The first feed given to the baby

questions.explanation: The afterbirth consists of the placenta and fetal membranes, which are expelled from the uterus by further contractions shortly after the baby is born. This is the third and final stage of labour.

questions.stem: What is the normal position of the baby just before birth?

options.text: Head up, feet pointing towards the cervix
Lying sideways across the uterus
Curled up with back towards the cervix
Head down, facing towards the cervix

questions.explanation: In a normal delivery, the baby is positioned head down with the head facing the cervix. This allows the head to pass through the dilated cervix first. A baby positioned feet-first (breech) may require special medical attention.

questions.stem: What happens when the 'waters break' during labour?

options.text: Blood is released from the placenta
The cervix begins to dilate
The amniotic sac ruptures, releasing amniotic fluid
The umbilical cord is cut

questions.explanation: When the 'waters break', the amniotic sac surrounding the baby ruptures, releasing the amniotic fluid. This usually happens during early labour and is a sign that birth is approaching.

questions.stem: Why is the umbilical cord clamped and cut after birth?

options.text: To allow the baby to start breathing on its own
To prevent the baby from losing too much blood
To separate the baby from the placenta as it is no longer needed for gas exchange
To help the afterbirth be delivered more quickly

questions.explanation: Once born, the baby can breathe air with its own lungs, so the placenta is no longer needed for gas exchange and nutrient supply. The umbilical cord is clamped and cut to separate the baby from the placenta.
